Each node is shaded by how many maximal cliques contain it: C sits in both, so it has 2 and the darkest shading, while A, B and D have 1 each, as the table lists." width="100%"} For every node, how many maximal cliques it belongs to. Nodes in many cliques bridge several tightly knit groups (people in several close circles, proteins in several complexes), which makes this a simple overlap and brokerage indicator. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [nodes]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[Union[int, str]] | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional list of nodes (IDs or labels) to report. If `None` (default), all nodes. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict[int, int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Node ID to the number of maximal cliques containing it. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If a node does not exist. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Counts memberships in the maximal cliques of `find_cliques()`, as NetworkX's `number_of_cliques` does. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Node C sits in the triangle and in the edge C-D: ::: {#bc98cbf1 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) g.add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A"), ("C", "D")]) {g.get_label_from_id(n): k for n, k in g.number_of_cliques().items()} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {'A': 1, 'B': 1, 'C': 2, 'D': 1} ``` ::: :::
